title: codeset · learn anything, taught one-on-one
excerpt: Learn anything you want. A full course on the subject, taught one-on-one by an AI tutor and aimed at the work you actually came to do. Every lesson ends in something of your own. Free while it's early.
content_html:
Build something real · a full syllabus · one-on-one tutor

Learn it properly.Whatever “it” is.

Learn C by writing a shell, or Rust by building a key-value store. Every course comes with a full syllabus, and the tutor teaches all of it inside the thing you're building, one concept at a time.

Cost
Free credits to start

Setup
Nothing to install

Catalog
27 courses, 1,044 lessons

Getting started

What the first ten minutes look like.

Three screens, in this order, and then you're in lesson one.

  1. 01

    Find the subject

    Search the catalog and read the whole syllabus before you make an account. You get every module and every lesson in the order they come, so nothing behind the sign-in wall is a surprise.

    No account needed

  2. 02

    Say what you want to build

    The thing you want to end up with. A shell, a game, a scraper for the site you keep checking by hand. It's the only setup question you get.

    A short conversation

  3. 03

    Start lesson one

    The workspace opens with the starter files for that idea, and the tutor teaches lesson one inside them. Same syllabus as everyone else, taught through what you're making.

    Same session

You finish the course with the thing you built.

The workspace above is where the apply step from the lesson at the top of this page happens: same project, same files, opened in the browser with the editor and terminal already running. Dictionaries got taught there because the build in the demo needed them — pick a different one up there and this changes with it, which is the point.

That is the whole method. The syllabus decides what you have to learn, your project decides what each lesson looks like, and you keep the project.

Most of the catalog

A project and a workspace, generated from the idea you described. Editor, terminal and your files, already set up when lesson one opens, and the syllabus taught by building the thing.

Nothing to install

When there's no code

Some subjects here have none, and those courses drop the workspace. You say why you're taking the course, and the same full syllabus gets taught against the problems you came with.

No setup at all

Why not just ask ChatGPT?

For a one-off question, go and do that. The difference shows up over weeks, when you need to finish something and still be able to do it yourself afterwards.

What we mean by course

Three things have to be true.

Otherwise it's a chatbot with a syllabus stapled to it, and you already have one of those.

The whole syllabus gets covered

What you want out of the course doesn't get to decide what you skip. Every skill in it is placed somewhere, taught through your own work where it fits and bridged with a short exercise where it doesn't.

It looks at the work itself

The tutor reads the files you wrote and the output you got, not your account of them. It responds to what is there, including the mistake you haven't spotted yet.

Reading it isn't finishing it

Every concept goes lesson, then apply it in your project, then a short test you take without the tutor. That last part is what the stars come from, so progress means you could do it unaided rather than that you scrolled past it.

The same course as the lesson above, in the rail the studio keeps beside it. Every lesson with stars was taught inside the project and then tested with the tutor switched off, and the stars are that test's result — so the rail records what you can do unaided rather than what you opened.

Python Beginner Foundations

A practical introduction to Python that begins with small runnable examples and develops understanding of values, control flow, collections, functions, files, errors, and object-oriented design. Learners progressively combine these ideas to read, reason about, and write clear Python programs.

6 modules · 65 lessons

python

Intro to Machine Learning

Build an intuitive foundation in machine learning, including models, features, loss, training, and generalization. Use Python and scikit-learn to reason about supervised and unsupervised learning, evaluate models, and improve their performance.

6 modules · 61 lessons

rust

Intro to Rust

An introduction to Rust covering syntax, ownership, type safety, error handling, collections, traits, concurrency, and modular program design. Learners develop the reasoning skills needed to write reliable and maintainable Rust code.

6 modules · 62 lessons

Kubernetes: From Container to Production

Learn Kubernetes by following a single containerized service from its first cluster deployment through networking, configuration, storage, security, scaling, and production operations. The curriculum connects core Kubernetes resources to the practical reasoning required to run reliable workloads.

6 modules · 59 lessons

Refresh core Python syntax and regain practical fluency with functions, collections, exceptions, modules, debugging, and clean small-script design. Progress from fundamental language patterns to synthesizing reliable, readable Python programs.

2 modules · 8 lessons

C Programming Foundations

Learn the core concepts of C programming, from program structure and control flow to memory, pointers, data structures, and modular design. Develop the ability to reason about low-level behavior, manage resources, and synthesize robust C programs.

6 modules · 67 lessons

Generate a course →

The things you'd ask before signing up.

What does it cost?
Nothing to start. Every account gets 2,000 free credits, worth about forty lessons or a course you generate yourself with plenty left over, with no card and no trial clock. Past that, plans start at $14 a month, and the pricing page shows what a credit buys before you spend one.

Is this only for programmers?
No. Plenty of the catalog has no code in it at all, and those courses work the same way: a full syllabus taught one-on-one, aimed at what you said you wanted from it.

What if my subject isn't in the catalog?
Describe it and the tutor writes the syllabus, module by module, before you commit to any of it. Generating a course costs credits from the same free balance every account starts with, and what comes out is a course like the others: readable in full, and yours to start or discard.

Will it just hand me the answer?
It's built not to. When you get stuck it looks for the thing you've misunderstood and teaches that instead of pasting in a fix. It isn't flawless at this, but it's what the whole tutor is tuned around.

Do I have to install anything?
No. Courses with code run in a workspace in your browser, with the editor, terminal and files already set up when the first lesson opens. Courses without code need no setup at all.

How much time does it take?
One lesson at a time, and it holds your place exactly. Come back a week later and the tutor picks up mid-thought instead of asking you to explain your project again.

What's still rough?
It's early. Some courses go deeper than others, the tutor gets things wrong now and then, and the coding workspace still needs a laptop, though lessons and the tutor work on a phone. You'd be an early user, with everything that means.

Early access

Judge it by the syllabus.

codeset is early, and the honest version of this pitch is the thing itself: a tutor that reads the files you wrote, and a full syllabus taught inside what you're building. Find your subject, read its syllabus end to end without an account, and if it holds up you'll have started building in ten minutes.

content_html_zh:
Build something real · a full syllabus · one-on-one tutor

Learn it properly.Whatever “it” is.

Learn C by writing a shell, or Rust by building a key-value store. Every course comes with a full syllabus, and the tutor teaches all of it inside the thing you're building, one concept at a time.

CostFree credits to start

SetupNothing to install

Catalog27 courses, 1,044 lessons

入门

What the first ten minutes look like.

Three screens, in this order, and then you're in lesson one.

  1. 01Find the subjectSearch the catalog and read the whole syllabus before you make an account. You get every module and every lesson in the order they come, so nothing behind the sign-in wall is a surprise.No account needed
  2. 02Say what you want to buildThe thing you want to end up with. A shell, a game, a scraper for the site you keep checking by hand. It's the only setup question you get.A short conversation
  3. 03Start lesson oneThe workspace opens with the starter files for that idea, and the tutor teaches lesson one inside them. Same syllabus as everyone else, taught through what you're making.Same session

You finish the course with the thing you built.

The workspace above is where the apply step from the lesson at the top of this page happens: same project, same files, opened in the browser with the editor and terminal already running. Dictionaries got taught there because the build in the demo needed them — pick a different one up there and this changes with it, which is the point.

That is the whole method. The syllabus decides what you have to learn, your project decides what each lesson looks like, and you keep the project.

Most of the catalog

A project and a workspace, generated from the idea you described. Editor, terminal and your files, already set up when lesson one opens, and the syllabus taught by building the thing.

没有什么可安装的

When there's no code

Some subjects here have none, and those courses drop the workspace. You say why you're taking the course, and the same full syllabus gets taught against the problems you came with.

No setup at all

显而易见的问题

Why not just ask ChatGPT?

For a one-off question, go and do that. The difference shows up over weeks, when you need to finish something and still be able to do it yourself afterwards.

What we mean by course

Three things have to be true.

Otherwise it's a chatbot with a syllabus stapled to it, and you already have one of those.

The whole syllabus gets covered

What you want out of the course doesn't get to decide what you skip. Every skill in it is placed somewhere, taught through your own work where it fits and bridged with a short exercise where it doesn't.

It looks at the work itself

The tutor reads the files you wrote and the output you got, not your account of them. It responds to what is there, including the mistake you haven't spotted yet.

Reading it isn't finishing it

Every concept goes lesson, then apply it in your project, then a short test you take without the tutor. That last part is what the stars come from, so progress means you could do it unaided rather than that you scrolled past it.

The same course as the lesson above, in the rail the studio keeps beside it. Every lesson with stars was taught inside the project and then tested with the tutor switched off, and the stars are that test's result — so the rail records what you can do unaided rather than what you opened.

A practical introduction to Python that begins with small runnable examples and develops understanding of values, control flow, collections, functions, files, errors, and object-oriented design. Learners progressively combine these ideas to read, reason about, and write clear Python programs.

An introduction to Rust covering syntax, ownership, type safety, error handling, collections, traits, concurrency, and modular program design. Learners develop the reasoning skills needed to write reliable and maintainable Rust code.

Learn Kubernetes by following a single containerized service from its first cluster deployment through networking, configuration, storage, security, scaling, and production operations. The curriculum connects core Kubernetes resources to the practical reasoning required to run reliable workloads.

6 modules · 59 lessons
